Arbelos Concyclic

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: A big half-circle holds two smaller ones, and a circle fits in the gap between them. Move the join between the two small arcs and see four dots stay on one circle.
How to play: Drag the dot C along the bottom line, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press a button to jump to another place, and tick a box to show more circles or names.
Look for the math

Move C and the whole picture changes shape. Yet the four dots A, C, F, D keep sitting on one circle, and B, C, E, D keep sitting on another. What fixes those circles in place?

The three arcs and the circle in the gap

The arbelos is bounded by three half-circles: on AB, on AC and on CB. The circle tucked into the gap touches them at D (the big arc), E (the left arc) and F (the right arc). Write a = AC and b = CB. Solving the three touching conditions gives its radius

r = a b (a+b) / (2 (a² + a b + b²))

The point C can slide anywhere at least 10 units from A or B, just as the applet allowed. The logic test checks the three touches at every one of 321 positions.

Two circles through four points

Let M be the top of the half-circle on AC and N the top of the one on CB. Then MC = a/√2 and NC = b/√2, and the two dashed circles drawn here are exactly the ones the page claims:

A, C, F, D lie on the circle with centre M and radius MC.
B, C, E, D lie on the circle with centre N and radius NC.

Both statements hold at all 321 draggable positions and at 1000 random ones. MA = MC and NB = NC are immediate; the surprising part is that the tangency points F and D (or E and D) land on those circles too.

Why the fourth point belongs

Invert about A with power AB × AC. This swaps B and C, leaves the small circle on CB where it is, and turns the big arc into an upright line at B. The inscribed circle becomes a circle touching two upright lines, and F becomes N. A line through B, N and the inverted point D′ comes back as a circle through A, C, F and D: a line through the centre of an inversion always inverts to a circle through that centre. The angle at N is 45°, so the returning circle meets AB at 45° too, which puts its centre at M.

A straightedge-and-compass build

The same diagram gives an easy construction: draw the circles about M with radius MC and about N with radius NC. They meet at C and at D, the tangency point on the big arc. A third circle, centred at L1 (the mirror of the big arc's top L in AB) and through A and B, passes through E and F as well — tick Show the third circle to see it. All of this uses only a straightedge and compass, as noted by P. Y. Woo.

About the original

The Java applet offered two ticks, "names" and "hint", and one blue point to drag. Its drawing has one arithmetic slip: it built its helper for the big arc with radius AB instead of the drawn radius AB/2, so its own inscribed circle and its points E, F, D came out about twice too large for the gap. This page follows the construction stated on the cut-the-knot page, which is the true circle touching all three arcs; the logic test checks the applet's version against it and records the difference. The statement itself is due to L. Bankoff, with the proof here adapted from Woo.

Press C in the middle, then drag C close to A. One claim circle shrinks with the left half and the other grows with the right half, but each keeps its four dots.
